If you know Java, here are key differences:

import com.example.Utils
import scala.math._                    // import all from scala.math
import scala.collection.mutable.{Map, Set}  // selective import

// Collections
List(1, 2, 3).map(_ * 2)              // List(2, 4, 6)
(1 to 10).filter(_ % 2 == 0)          // Range of even numbers
Set(1, 2, 3).contains(2)              // true
Map("a" -> 1).get("a")                // Some(1)

// String operations
"hello".toUpperCase()                 // "HELLO"
"hello world".split(" ")              // Array("hello", "world")
"hello".length                        // 5

// Math
scala.math.abs(-5)                    // 5
scala.math.sqrt(16)                   // 4.0
scala.math.max(1, 5)                  // 5

// Option (null safety)
Option(value).getOrElse(default)
Some(5).map(_ * 2)                    // Some(10)
None.getOrElse(0)                     // 0

val x = 5
val result = x match {
  case 1 => "one"
  case 2 => "two"
  case n if n > 10 => "big"
  case _ => "other"
}

val nums = List(1, 2, 3, 4, 5)

nums.map(_ * 2)                       // List(2, 4, 6, 8, 10)
nums.filter(_ > 2)                    // List(3, 4, 5)
nums.fold(0)(_ + _)                   // 15 (sum)
nums.find(_ > 3)                      // Some(4)
nums.exists(_ > 4)                    // true
nums.forall(_ > 0)                    // true
: Scala's pattern matching is exhaustiveness-checked by the compiler. It's safer than Java's casting.
: Quick way to define data containers with equality, hashing, and pattern matching built-in.

case class Person(name: String, age: Int)
val alice = Person("Alice", 30)
alice.name           // "Alice"
: Scala infers types from context. Annotations are mainly for clarity or API boundaries.
Tuple indices are 1-based (like Lua, unlike arrays)
: If you need reference equality, use

val a = new String("hello")
val b = new String("hello")
a == b                                // true (value equality)
a eq b                                // false (reference equality)

val nums = List(1, 2, 3)
val result = nums.map { x =>
  if (x > 1) x * 2
  else x
}
println(result)
is an expression in Scala (not a statement). It always returns a value, even if you don't explicitly return.
